title: How Many Nodes Are K Steps Away
statement:
All node values of a binary tree are **different**. `target` is the value of one node in the tree. The **distance** between two nodes is the number of edges on the path between them; the path may go **up** to a parent as well as down to children.

Return the number of nodes whose distance from the target node is **exactly `k`**.
constraints: values are different integers between 0 and 100000; `target` is the value of a node in the tree

examples.explanation: From 4 the path 4, 2, 1, 3, 6 (or 7) has 4 edges: the nodes 6 and 7.
The children of the root: 2 and 3.

hints.nudge: From the target you can walk DOWN easily, but a tree has no link to the parent. Which nodes above the target would you need to remember, and what is the distance to them?
hints.pattern: Either build parent links (or an undirected graph) and run a breadth-first search for k steps from the target; or a single recursion that returns the distance to the target and counts nodes in the 'other side' subtrees at the remaining distance.
hints.pseudocode:
BFS version: parent[node] = its parent; queue = [target node]; repeat k times: replace the queue by all unvisited neighbours (left, right, parent); return the size of the queue
Recursive version: go(node) returns the distance from node to the target if the target is in its subtree, else -1; on the way up count nodes of the opposite subtree at depth k - distance - 1
hints.walkthrough: Treat the tree as an undirected graph: every node is connected to its two children and its parent. Record the parent of each node in one traversal, locate the target node, then do a breadth-first search from the target for exactly k rounds, never visiting a node twice; the nodes in the queue after k rounds are exactly the nodes at distance k. In the recursive alternative, every node that has the target in its subtree at distance d from it (d < k) can reach nodes in its OTHER child's subtree at depth k - d - 1 below that child; the node itself is at distance k when d = k; and nodes below the target at depth k are counted when the target is found. Both versions visit each node a constant number of times: O(n).
